newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands walk out over sick pay cuts at Mercedes.
newsitem.headline: Thousands walk out over sick pay cuts at Mercedes.

text.p: Around 10,000 workers at Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes plant in Stuttgart walked out on Tuesday to protest against cuts to sick pay and other benefits that take effect from the start of the month.
The car workers were joined by members of unions representing construction and white-collar workers and by a group of some 600 delegates from the OeTV transport and public sector union.

Helmut Lense, chairman of the Mercedes works council at the Untertuerkheim plant in Stuttgart, accused Daimler-Benz of using "the personnel policies of Rambo" for applying a newly-passed law to cut sick payments from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent without consultation with unions.
"We can promise the board that this is only the beginning," Lense said at a protest outside the Mercedes factory.

He said workers would refuse to work overtime and additional shifts until Daimler-Benz, one of the first companies to put the new law into effect, acknowledged that they could not override sick pay clauses in existing contracts.
Daimler has said it was confident of making up for production lost so far as a result of disruption, which started with protest actions at Mercedes plants at the weekend.

Gerhard Zambelli, regional head of the IG Metall metal union, said he had also received notice from Daimler-Benz management that they were also cancelling agreements on Christmas money and bonus payments.
Christmas pay for Mercedes has normally been payable at a minimum 50 percent of monthly wages.
"The autumn is getting hotter all the time," Zambelli said, referring to earlier union threats that strike action could not be ruled out ahead of the next round of wage talks.
The Stuttgart demonstration was one of a number of protests around Germany against the cuts in benefits envisaged by a law introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition earlier this month.

According to work council representatives, some 7,000 workers walked out at the Bochum plant of General Motors' Adam Opel unit, while some 12,000 early-shift workers at Ford's German plant in Cologne also held a meeting in protest at the cuts.
